reviews.question: Which of the following statements is true?

options.b: Dynamic friction is always greater than static friction
options.c: Dynamic friction is always the same as static friction

reviews.explanation: Kinetic(dynamic) friction resists relative sliding of the surfaces. Static friction is self-adjusting: 0 ≤ fₛ ≤ μₛN, whereas the approximate Coulomb model gives fₖ = μₖN during sliding. For many material pairs μₖ < μₛ, so kinetic friction is smaller than the maximum or limiting static friction at the same normal load. It need not be smaller than the actual static friction, which may be zero. Moreover the inequality between the coefficients is empirical, not an absolute rule. Thus none of the four statements containing “always” or a fixed factor is generally true. The printed answer(a) reflects an intended comparison with limiting static friction, but the printed wording does not state that qualification.

reviews.question: The maximum value of ______, which acts when a body just begins to slide over another body, is known as ______.
reviews.explanation: The maximum static friction at impending sliding is limiting friction. Static friction develops between mating surfaces under external force without relative sliding. Dynamic friction develops when there is relative sliding; it is also called kinetic friction. Approximate Coulomb laws: (1) Friction acts tangentially and opposes relative sliding or its tendency.(2) Static friction varies from zero to its limiting value according to forces tending to cause sliding.(3) Limiting friction bears a constant ratioμₛ to the normal reaction for given surfaces and conditions.(4) It is approximately independent of apparent contact area and shape.(5) It depends on the nature and condition of the surfaces, including roughness or smoothness.(6) At low sliding speeds kinetic friction is approximately speed-independent. At higher speeds it can vary; a slight reduction is sometimes observed but is not a universal law.
reviews.note: Retained key e; corrected “kinematic” to “kinetic” and qualified the high-speed claim while preserving all six laws.

reviews.sourceExplanation: The maximum value of static friction, which comes into play, when a body just begins to slide over the surface of the other body, is known as limiting friction. Static Friction—The static friction is the frictional force that develops between mating surface when subjected to external force but there is no relative motion between them. Dynamic Friction—The dynamic friction is the frictional force that develops between mating surface when subjected to external forces and there is relative motion between them. The dynamic friction is also known as kinematic friction. Laws of Solid Friction[Static or Dynamic]: 1. Friction acts tangential to the surface in contact and is in a direction opposite to that in which motion is to impend i. e. take place.2. Friction force is maximum at the instant of impending motion. Its variation from zero to maximum value[Limiting friction] depends upon the resultant force tending to cause motion.3. The magnitude of limiting friction bears a constant ratio to the normal reaction between the mating surface.4. Limiting friction is independent of the area and shape of contact surface.5. Limiting friction depends upon the nature(roughness or smoothness) of the surface in contact.6. At low velocities between sliding surface, the friction force is practically independent of the velocity. However, slight reduction in friction occurs when the speed are high.

reviews.question: What is the moment of inertia of a semicircular lamina with the base horizontal about the centroidal axis parallel to the x-axis, if the radius is R?
reviews.explanation:
Moment of inertia of a semicircular section:
We know that the MOI of a semicircular section about base AC is equal to half of the MOI of a circular section about AC.
I_AC = (1/2)(πd⁴/64) = πR⁴/8 ≈ 0.393R⁴.

We also know that the area of the semicircular section is
A = (1/2)πR² = πR²/2,
and the distance between the centre of gravity of the section and the base AC is
h = 4R/(3π).

The MOI of the section through its C.G. and parallel to the x–x axis is
I_G = I_AC − Ah²
    = [πR⁴/8] − [(πR²/2)(4R/(3π))²]
    = πR⁴/8 − 8R⁴/(9π)
    ≈ 0.1097R⁴.

Note: The MOI about the y–y axis will be the same as that about base AC, i.e. πR⁴/8 ≈ 0.393R⁴.
reviews.note: Complete source including y-axis note retained. Exact coefficient 0.10975696.

Their centres are(x₁, y₁)=(10, 40) mm and(x₂, y₂)=(40, 90) mm. x̄=(a₁x₁+a₂x₂)/(a₁+a₂)=[80×20×10+80×20×40]/[80×20+80×20]=25 mm. ȳ=(a₁y₁+a₂y₂)/(a₁+a₂)=[80×20×40+80×20×90]/[80×20+80×20]=65 mm. Thus centroid(25, 65) mm.

reviews.question: The centre of gravity of a plane lamina is not at its geometrical centre if it is a
reviews.explanation: For a uniform lamina under uniform gravity, the centre of gravity coincides with its geometric area centroid, including for a right triangle. A circle, square and rectangle additionally have a centre of symmetry there. A right triangle generally lacks central symmetry, but its centroid remains a geometric centre. The source statement is false if “geometrical centre” means centroid, and undefined if another centre is meant. Choice(d) answers a different question about lacking central symmetry.

reviews.question: Which represents neutral equilibrium?

options.b: Smooth cylinder on a curved surface
options.c: Smooth cylinder on a convex surface

reviews.explanation: Neutral equilibrium means a small allowed displacement leaves potential energy unchanged and the centre of gravity at constant height. A cube balanced on an edge is unstable; an ordinary cylinder on top of a convex support is unstable. A cylinder in an ordinary concave trough is stable transversely. But(b) says only “curved surface, ”without shape, orientation or permitted displacement, so it cannot be classified. If(b) meant an ordinary concave trough, the intended answer is(d); a standard neutral example is a cylinder on a horizontal plane. The printed unspecified geometry prevents a definite unique classification.
